We'll see some erosion in that as I suspect we're going to be able to hang on to loan growth as we've guided the past couple of quarters. So, yes, I think we're still looking at 6%, 7% something like that. We're 7% annualized for this most recent quarter and boy in my mind, good solid deposit growth is call it 2%. So, yes, that's a pretty widespread and that's going to begin to erode into our loans and deposit ratio, which makes me feel good. We are where we are at this point.

If the Fed continues, probably similar results and if the curve does steepen, that's where we'll pick up a little bit more than what we've been experiencing in the past in terms of the margin.

Got it. So you do expect the margin to continue to trend higher. Can you discuss the competition for deposits on both the consumer and commercial sides on the island? Is it increasing? Are you feeling any pressure to raise your deposit rates for retail customers?

Yes. I'd say that it depends on the segment that you're talking about. I think both the commercial at this point and consumer lower-end segment, so smaller deposit relationships have been priced pretty rationally. But obviously when you get into the larger client types where there's just an awful lot of money at stake, people are bidding on a one-off custom basis for time deposits. We're seeing that in the market.

Thank you. And our next question is from line of Aaron Deer of Sandler O'Neill. Your line is open.

Hi, good morning, everyone. Peter, given your outlook for loan or deposit growth heading into next year, I guess that would suggest that you're going to be using cash flows coming off the investment securities to fund loan growth. Our expectations for earning asset growth will depend on deposit growth. If we see low single-digit growth in deposits, that will reflect our expected earning asset growth.

Right.

That's all related to the carrying cost for the Visa sale.

Hi, good morning, everyone. Just touching base on the good differential you had in the securities purchases in the quarter. Okay, so no shift in purchases or anything if the increase on a linked quarter basis between last quarter's differential and this quarter's differential was purely market-driven and rate-driven.

Yes, duration is flat.

Duration is flat, yes.

Net income for the full year 2011 was $2.63 per share, down from $3.07 in the previous year. Although net income declined year-over-year, we observed positive developments in several of our key subsidiaries. Before discussing our individual businesses, I want to touch on Loews' strategic management. We adhere to three core strategic principles aimed at building long-term shareholder value. First, we focus on making strategic investments and acquisitions that position us for future growth. This past year, we did not make any acquisitions at the holding company level; however, we facilitated significant investments at our subsidiaries, Boardwalk and HighMount, which should greatly enhance their long-term value and, in turn, that of Loews. Our second principle is effectively managing and allocating Loews' capital. In 2011, we invested $718 million to repurchase 18.2 million shares of Loews' common stock, a move we believe significantly enhances value for all shareholders. Lastly, we continuously strive to improve our subsidiaries’ operating performance and capital structure. Throughout 2011, Loews and our subsidiaries navigated through economic challenges while positioning themselves for the future. Our subsidiaries made significant strides toward strengthening their businesses and operations to compete effectively in any economic climate, and I am pleased with their progress.  Starting with CNA, the company continues to pursue its strategic goals of enhancing market position and profitability in core operations. CNA is emphasizing underwriting and pricing discipline while seeking growth and strengthening its balance sheet. A few key points highlight CNA's success: First, positive rate increases, strong business retention, and robust new business have led to premium growth in the P&C sector. Second, 2011 marked the fifth consecutive year of favorable prior year P&C loss development for CNA. Third, by the end of 2011, CNA's book value per common share rose to $42.92, reflecting an improved capital position. Lastly, CNA is making efforts to streamline and strengthen its organization, having sold its 50% stake in First Insurance Company of Hawaii in August and acquired the minority shares of CNA Surety in June. Next, Diamond Offshore is enhancing its fleet capabilities while focusing on prudent capital allocation. The company recently announced plans to construct a deepwater semi-submersible rig, the Ocean Onyx, which is scheduled for delivery in the third quarter of 2013. Diamond sees substantial demand for new deepwater units, and this rig is intended to meet that need. The Ocean Onyx will be constructed using an existing hull from a cold stacked unit, allowing for a quicker and more cost-effective build. Over the last five years, Diamond has ordered, built, or purchased eight units capable of operating in deep or ultra-deepwater. Turning to Boardwalk, the company is experiencing significant growth as it seeks projects that leverage its core assets while diversifying services and geographic reach. Recently, Boardwalk announced major developments in the liquids-rich Eagle Ford shale, including the construction of 55 miles of gathering pipeline and a natural gas liquids processing plant, with long-term agreements already secured with Statoil and Talisman for half of the plant's capacity. The Boardwalk management team has identified approximately $875 million of growth and acquisition opportunities, including the Eagle Ford Shale project and the recent acquisition of HP Storage. Regarding HighMount and the natural gas market, we maintain a positive outlook on long-term natural gas prices, but HighMount has taken steps to diversify its business due to recent trends. The company has acquired oil and natural gas liquids-rich acreage, which currently offers better economics for drilling compared to natural gas. HighMount plans to initiate drilling this month in areas believed to contain oil-rich liquids and is also pursuing drilling programs aimed at achieving higher oil and liquid production. Finally, let's discuss Loews Hotels and welcome Paul Whetsell as the new President and CEO. With over 35 years in the hotel industry, Paul brings valuable experience to Loews Hotels. Paul will focus on growing Loews Hotels while ensuring exceptional service and unique properties. Now, I'll turn the call over to Pete Keegan.

Thanks, Jim, and good morning. Loews today reported net income of $268 million or $0.67 per share for the fourth quarter 2011 as compared to $466 million or $1.12 per share in the fourth quarter of 2010. The decrease in the fourth quarter was primarily due to lower investment income from limited partnership results of CNA and the increase to insurance reserves for CNA's payout annuity business. The fourth quarter also reflects lower earnings of Diamond Offshore. Loews' net income for the full year was $1.1 billion or $2.63 per share compared to $1.3 billion or $3.07 per share in 2010. Book value per share for Loews increased to $47.49 at December 31, 2011, as compared to $44.51 at December 31, 2010, approximately a 7% increase. CNA's contribution to Loews' net income for the fourth quarter was $192 million as compared to $297 million in 2010 and $569 million for the full year of 2011 compared to $609 million for the prior year. The decrease was due to lower investment income from limited partnership results of $57 million and a $104 million increase in insurance reserves through its payout annuity business. As discussed in the CNA call, the underlying core P&C business continued to show improvement in underwriting profitability and growth. CNA also continues its disciplined reserving practices. In the fourth quarter, the P&C business benefited from $250 million of pre-tax favorable prior year loss development. CNA has had 20 consecutive quarters of favorable prior year reserve development. Diamond Offshore's contribution to net income for the fourth quarter of 2011 was $88 million compared to $113 million in the prior year quarter and $451 million for the full year 2011 as compared to $446 million from the year before. Results for the fourth quarter were impacted by a higher number of planned downtime days for scheduled maintenance, surveys, mobilization, and upgrades, while the full year results benefited from historically low unanticipated equipment downtime. Boardwalk Pipeline's net income for the fourth quarter decreased to $21 million from $34 million in the prior-year quarter and $77 million for the full year in 2011 compared to $114 million from the prior year. The decrease is primarily attributable to one-time items in both 2011 and 2010. Absent those items, the quarter was basically flat year-over-year. Boardwalk recently raised $217 million in an equity offering. HighMount's net income for the fourth quarter decreased to $12 million from $21 million in the prior year quarter and $62 million for the full year in 2011 compared to $77 million from the prior year. Results are primarily due to decreased sales volumes stemming from a reduction in HighMount's drilling activity and declines in natural gas prices. HighMount's production volumes and realized prices in the fourth quarter are as follows: Natural gas production was 10.7 billion cubic feet at an average realized price of $5.71 per 1,000 cubic feet; natural gas liquids production was 656,000 barrels at an average realized price of $39.36 per barrel; and oil production was 72,000 barrels at an average price of $88.74 per barrel. HighMount has hedges in place for about 52% of its total production for 2012 at an average price of $5.79 and has hedges in place for about 16% of its total production for 2013 at an average price of $5.44. During the fourth quarter, HighMount refinanced its outstanding debt, which included a $400 million capital contribution from Loews. Loews Hotels had improved results for the quarter and year. Net income increased to $5 million for the fourth quarter in 2011 from breakeven in the prior year. For the full year in 2011, net income rose to $13 million as compared to $1 million for 2010. The improved results were due to the improvement of business in leisure travel, with particularly strong results for Loews at the Miami Beach and Orlando Hotels. Holding company cash and investments as of December 31, 2011, totaled $3.3 billion as compared to $4 billion at September 30, 2011. In the fourth quarter, we made capital contributions of $400 million to HighMount for the refinancing of its term loans and $106 million to fund the acquisition of working interest in oil and gas properties. In addition, we invested $285 million for an 80% equity ownership in a joint venture with Boardwalk Pipeline. It gives us a barometer on how CNA is doing and it helps all Loews shareholders to value CNA as well. Beyond that, whether the float is 10% or 5% or 20%, I don't think it's worthwhile for me to comment.

The next question comes from David Adelman of Morgan Stanley.

Jim and Pete, well, first, were there any dynamics that limited at all the window of opportunity for Loews to buy back its common stock during the fourth quarter?

I'm not going to answer that question because I don't want to speculate. If there were any corporate activities, that would be one thing, but if there weren't, it doesn't make sense for us to discuss potential reasons that might have influenced our decision to buy shares.

Okay. Can you comment, in general, about what you see in terms of the opportunity for the holding company to make acquisitions in the present environment?

Yes. I think, and I felt this way for a few years now, that the acquisitions in this environment are very difficult for a few reasons. Number one, because the future is really not clear. I don't have a clear view of whether the economy is going to grow at 2%, 4%, or 0%. And there still are an enormous number of uncertainties that those of us that manage businesses have to deal with day in and day out. That's number one. And number two, there really aren't a lot of properties or assets that are for sale at prices that I think would be attractive for Loews shareholders. So we don't feel any strong urge or itch to go out and do a big deal.

Okay. Pete, I have two specific financial questions if you have the information available. I'm interested in the general partner dividend payment at the Boardwalk General Partner for the full year. A couple of quick questions, numbers of questions in HighMount and then some more subset in the questions about the fundamentals there. What are your carrying values at year-end for it, with the increased divestments? Were there any write-downs at all?

Okay. So the carrying value just goes up by the two new investments in?

Effectively, yes.

Could you please give me the numbers again? You were going quickly, and I didn't catch them.

For HighMount, we contributed $106 million for acquisitions and invested $400 million in capital, which helped reduce the debt from $1.1 billion to $700 million.

So $506 million is what the carrying value goes out by?

That's the amount we put in. That's correct.

Okay. Jim, you seemed more enthusiastic about that business when discussing trends, especially with gas prices having decreased significantly. First, let's revisit basic economics. For demand to rise, prices need to fall; however, our prices are increasing, which we find encouraging. Currently, the spot gas price is about $2.50 per Mcf, equivalent to approximately $15 per barrel of oil. Oil prices are currently $97 per barrel for West Texas Intermediate and $115 per barrel for Brent Crude, making gas very inexpensive. We have observed several years where gas has traded at less than 30% of the price of oil, which I think is leading people to consider switching from oil to natural gas. Recently, I spoke to someone who invested several hundred thousand dollars to convert his commercial building in New York City from heating oil to natural gas. There are various projects underway to provide natural gas, either as compressed gas or LNG, at service stations for trucks, delivery vehicles, and personal cars. Additionally, we expect the closure of many coal-fired power plants, which will be replaced by natural gas facilities. It’s clear to me that natural gas consumption will significantly increase over the next four to five years. Furthermore, in the coming years, new LNG export facilities will be able to manage about 1.5% of daily natural gas production, signaling additional demand for natural gas to the market. I believe many factors will contribute to increased natural gas demand. However, since most of these initiatives require substantial capital investments, it may take time to materialize. Yet, I am confident that this growth will occur, as we have seen natural gas consumption increase at a much faster rate than oil consumption in the United States recently, and I expect that trend to continue.

So am I correct in thinking that with your investment of $500 million into this business and your initial remarks, it appears you are enthusiastic about this segment? What potential returns do you anticipate over the next three to five years? Is that an accurate understanding?

Yes, we have invested $100 million in land acquisitions in Oklahoma, primarily focused on oil, and we find the economics of the drilling program very appealing. In this context, CNA is indeed very strong in terms of capital ratings, which would typically classify it as a AA-rated insurance company. Under Tom Motamed's leadership, CNA has ambitious growth plans. We expect to see price increases this year, and we are also aiming to increase our market share volumes. Therefore, over the next few years, we anticipate that what appears to be excess surplus at CNA will be utilized to support increased written premiums.

That's correct.

We haven't concentrated on that. Our focus has been on growing HighMount's business and diversifying into oil and natural gas liquids, along with establishing a consistent production stream for those liquids. It will take us more time to fully diversify HighMount's production. Therefore, we are not considering what steps we need to take to take this company public; that is not currently on our agenda.

And one last question on the fundamentals of gas. You remain to be very positive about long-term outlook, and we finally started to see the gas rig count decline. Is there anything in the marketplace that tells you that the covenants that various companies have there, that have been very aggressive in drilling and have a lot of debt, that we may actually get to a place where there will be forced shutdowns anytime soon? I haven't seen anything specific, but my instinct tells me that there are a significant number of independent gas E&P companies that are going to have a lot of trouble. With gas trading at $3.5 or $4, the industry was going to operate at minus $25 billion cash flow. I mean, they were going to have to raise $25 billion from outside sources. And now with spot gas prices at $2.50 and hedges running off for E&P companies, I think there is, in some boardrooms, concern that's moving to fear that's going to move to panic. I think that the decline in rigs is just one symptom of that. Now we'll have to see how this all plays out over the next six months to a year, but it looks like we are going to end the heating season with record amounts of natural gas that's going to put some pressure on natural gas prices. We're also seeing the time spreads increasing because people think that natural gas will go up in the future, which will benefit Boardwalk Pipeline. However, I think that it's going to take some time, measured in a number of quarters, for natural gas to really hit bottom and start to move up. And as that happens, there will be more discipline on the part of gas E&P companies so that they won't go out with such reckless abandon in terms of their drilling program.

Your next question comes from Michael Millman of Millman Research Associates.

I guess some more HighMount. Could you give us some idea of when you first bought HighMount, what you thought it would be worth long term, long term might have been as much as 20 years? And to what extent that number might have changed considering us going out, considering that fracking is unleashing lots of reserves, although I guess, they were just produced?

A good question, Mike. When we acquired HighMount, natural gas prices were around $7.5 to $7.75 per Mcf. In the first year, they nearly doubled to about $15 per Mcf. Now, gas prices have fallen by approximately 80% to under $3 per Mcf. At these levels, nobody is making money. Even though HighMount isn't a public company, the value of our investment is clearly lower now compared to when we made the investment. We did not foresee the significant impact that fracking would have on natural gas supply, and I don't think anyone fully understood that impact either. However, since then, the cost of exploring for natural gas, along with the prices of rigs and other services, has decreased. Still, at $2.50 or $3 per Mcf, very few can explore for natural gas or dry gas profitably. My prediction is that natural gas prices will rise in the upcoming quarters and years, eventually reaching an equilibrium price that will likely remain lower than what we initially expected when investing in HighMount. Despite that, I am optimistic about HighMount’s future and the investment opportunities available, and I believe we will be able to achieve good returns on our investment.

Good. Switching to hotels. You mentioned asset-like; I think, most of the hotels you currently own, you're talking about doing franchising or managing hotels or some combination?

No. We're not thinking of franchising per se. We are in the ownership and management business, and we think that we should be able to increase the number of hotels that we have by putting some equity money in, but having partners in ownership. And likewise, we are also going to be looking to increase the number of just hotels that we have under management.

Your next question comes from Sam Yake, BGB Securities. James S. Tisch, Chief Executive Officer, stated that they are not considering franchising in a traditional sense. Their focus remains on ownership and management, with plans to grow their hotel portfolio through equity investments while partnering with others in ownership. Additionally, they aim to expand the number of hotels they manage.

I'm curious, when you assess potential investments for Loews, do you have a rigorous process for comparing those investments to the option of repurchasing more Loews stock?

Absolutely, positively. When we buy a business that we don't know, there's a lot of uncertainty to it. And the thing that we happen to know best is Loews, and because three of our subsidiaries are public, we have a very good sense of what those businesses are worth. So when we buy back our shares, we don't have to pay a premium. We're able to buy it at market price. Then when we buy another company, typically, you have to pay a premium to the market price. So all of that and more figures into the calculus that we go through when we think about buying a new business versus buying in our own shares.

It seems to me that given the recent trading of the stock, there are very few potential investments that could measure up. When you mentioned scaling back your stock repurchase in the fourth quarter, have you considered implementing a 10b5-1 plan to navigate around some restrictions?

I didn't say we have to scale back our share repurchases. What I said is that I'm not going to comment about our share repurchases. And I'll just say that our lawyers here are aware of the current state-of-the-art in technology in share repurchases, and we consider all of that when we do buy our shares.

Okay. I have one last big picture question. When I look back at Loews' history and see your long-term success, especially with the strategic transaction where you spun off boulevard in a tax-efficient manner that benefited shareholders, I wonder what factors you consider when thinking about potentially doing a similar deal with one of your subsidiaries.

We consistently emphasize our commitment to creating long-term value for all shareholders, which is what motivates our daily activities. We strive to eliminate bias in our analysis of opportunities and focus on identifying transactions that enhance shareholder value. As we gain insights and knowledge about various transactions, we determine the best execution strategies to maximize that value. It's a lengthy process that requires hard work, research, and thoroughness.

Thank you. This concludes the Q&A portion of today's call. I will now turn the call back to Mary Skafidas for any closing remarks.

Thanks, Kelly, and thank you all for your continued interest. A replay of this call is going to be available in approximately two hours. This concludes our call for today.

Thank you. This concludes today's conference. You may now disconnect.
